source_title: Unmanned Aircraft System Defined; Preemption for Unmanned Aircraft Systems; Operations
regulated_party: Counties, municipalities, and other political subdivisions
regulated_activity: Enacting or enforcing an ordinance, resolution, regulation, or policy regulating UAS testing or operation
requirement_type: Prohibition (local measures void), with three carve-outs
summary: O.C.G.A. § 6-1-4(a) defines 'unmanned aircraft system' as a powered aerial vehicle that does not carry a human operator, is operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within/on the aircraft, uses aerodynamic forces for lift, can fly autonomously or be piloted remotely, and can be expendable or recoverable (excluding satellites). Subsection (b) provides that any local ordinance, resolution, regulation, or policy regulating UAS testing or operation is preempted and void, except that a political subdivision may (1) enforce an ordinance adopted on or before April 1, 2017, (2) adopt an ordinance enforcing FAA restrictions, or (3) adopt an ordinance providing for or prohibiting UAS launch/intentional landing from/on its own public property (except as to commercial UAS operation). Subsection (c) allows the state itself, through agency/departmental rules, to provide for or prohibit UAS launch/landing on its own public property.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Georgia's preemption is broad and well-established (in force since 2017) — AEC operators should generally not expect a significant municipal UAS-ordinance patchwork, though confirm whether a specific project site is government-owned public property subject to a launch/landing ordinance under the narrow local or state carve-outs.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: A local ordinance purporting to independently regulate UAS testing or operation outside the three statutory exceptions is void by operation of state law; confirm whether a pre-April-2017 local ordinance remains grandfathered for any specific project site.
verification_status: Full current statutory text (subsections a-c, pre-2025 amendment) verified directly against Justia's codification of the 2024 Georgia Code.

geographic_scope: Statewide (400 ft buffer around ticketed entertainment events; also authorizes local ordinances for mass public gatherings)
source_title: HB 58 (2025) — Ticketed Entertainment Event UAS Restriction and Local Mass-Gathering Ordinance Authorization
citation: O.C.G.A. § 6-1-4, as amended by HB 58 (2025 Regular Session), Ga. Laws 2025
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 400 ft of, or above, a 'ticketed entertainment event' (a gated event requiring a revocable license for attendance)
summary: HB 58, effective July 1, 2025, amended O.C.G.A. § 6-1-4 to (1) prohibit operating a UAS within 400 ft of or above a 'ticketed entertainment event' — a gated event requiring a revocable license for attendance, capturing music festivals, sporting events, and performing-arts events that fall below the 30,000-seat federal stadium-TFR threshold — as a misdemeanor, with exceptions for consent from event authorities, FAA-regulation-compliant operations, an employee's official-business flights, and a property owner flying over their own property consistent with federal rules; and (2) authorize local governments to adopt ordinances, resolutions, regulations, or policies restricting UAS flight specifically over mass public gatherings, a narrow additional carve-out to the general preemption in GA-001. The Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency (GEMA) has confirmed this restriction applies to major ticketed events such as FIFA World Cup matches hosted in Georgia.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any AEC project near a scheduled ticketed entertainment event (festival grounds, stadium-adjacent construction, temporary event infrastructure) as requiring either 400+ ft standoff or documented consent from event organizers/authorities before flying; separately check whether the relevant local government has adopted a mass-gathering-specific UAS ordinance under this new local-authority carve-out.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the specific consent obtained from event authorities for any flight within 400 ft of a ticketed event, and confirm whether a local mass-gathering ordinance applies to the project site now that GA-001's preemption has been narrowed for this purpose; the exact codified subsection lettering for this 2025 amendment was not independently verified against Justia's codification in this pass (Justia's public database had not yet reflected the amendment as of the research date), so confirm current subsection numbering before citing to a client.
verification_status: Substance and effective date corroborated by Georgia's own Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency (GEMA) drone FAQ page and multiple secondary industry-compliance sources describing HB 58; the exact enrolled bill text and resulting codified subsection lettering were not independently read in full in this pass (Justia's codification had not yet been updated to reflect the amendment).

geographic_scope: Statewide (applicable at/near any place of incarceration)
source_title: Use of Unmanned Aircraft to Deliver Contraband or Photograph a Place of Incarceration
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to deliver or attempt to deliver contraband/prohibited items to an inmate; using a UAS to intentionally photograph or record a place of incarceration for purposes of committing a criminal offense
requirement_type: Prohibition (felony), with a prior-authorization option for noncriminal photography
permit_or_approval_required: No — but photography with prior warden/superintendent authorization is not a violation
summary: O.C.G.A. § 42-5-18(f) makes it unlawful to intentionally use a UAS to violate the section's contraband-delivery prohibitions (subsection (b), covering weapons, intoxicating liquor, drugs, and telecommunications devices; and (b.1), covering tobacco), or to intentionally photograph or record images of a place of incarceration via UAS for purposes of committing a criminal offense. A person may secure prior authorization from the warden or superintendent (or designee) to photograph/record as evidence of noncriminal intent, though failure to obtain such authorization does not itself evidence criminal intent. Violations are felonies: 1-10 years' imprisonment for contraband delivery, and 1-5 years' imprisonment for unauthorized criminal-intent photography/recording. 'Unmanned aircraft system' incorporates the § 6-1-4 definition (GA-001).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Obtain prior written authorization from the warden or superintendent before conducting any AEC inspection, mapping, or documentation flight at or near a Georgia correctional facility, jail, or detention center — this creates a clean evidentiary record of noncriminal intent even though the statute is intent-based and authorization is not strictly mandatory for lawful commercial work.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the protected facility's owner, operator, administrator, commander, or other official identified by the authority before mobilization and ask whether the proposed AEC mission qualifies for written approval or an employment/contractor exception. Provide the site, purpose, dates, flight area, crew and aircraft details the facility requests, and retain the signed authorization and security conditions; do not assume ordinary site access or a client work order is sufficient.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the specific facility authorization obtained (warden/superintendent name, date, scope) for any correctional-facility-adjacent UAS work, given the felony exposure; confirm the target facility qualifies as a 'place of incarceration' under the broad statutory definition (state, federal, local, or privately operated).
verification_status: Full current statutory text (subsection (f) and cross-referenced definitions) verified directly against Justia's codification of the Georgia Code.

issuing_authority: Georgia General Assembly / Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Wildlife Resources Division
source_title: Restrictions on Hunting Aids and Electronic Equipment Applicable to UAS (DNR Interpretation)
source_type: Binding law or regulation, with agency interpretation extending scope to UAS
binding_level: Binding (statutory text); DNR's UAS-specific application is an agency interpretation, not explicit statutory language
regulated_party: Any person hunting or facilitating hunting
regulated_activity: Using electronic communications equipment to facilitate pursuit of wildlife (§ 27-3-12(a)); hunting wildlife or feral hogs from an aircraft (§ 27-3-13, with a feral-hog motor-vehicle exception under permit)
requirement_type: Prohibition, with a limited feral-hog exception
summary: O.C.G.A. § 27-3-12(a) makes it unlawful to use electronic communications equipment for the purpose of facilitating pursuit of any wild animal, game bird, or game animal (this subsection does not name drones/UAS explicitly). O.C.G.A. § 27-3-13 separately makes it unlawful to hunt wildlife or feral hogs from an aircraft (among other named vehicle types), except that feral hogs may be hunted from motor vehicles under an applicable wildlife-control permit. Secondary sources report that Georgia DNR's Wildlife Resources Division interprets and applies these provisions (together with a broader agency position prohibiting aircraft use, including drones, to hunt, capture, kill, or harass wildlife) to prohibit using a UAS to drive, locate, or direct a hunter to game, with feral-hog location remaining the one lawful hunting-adjacent drone use under DNR's current guidance.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid any activity that could be read by DNR as locating, driving, or directing a hunter to game, since the agency applies these hunting-equipment statutes to UAS even though the core statutory text does not name drones explicitly.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the survey/mapping purpose of any UAS flight over wildlife habitat or hunting-adjacent land to distinguish it from a hunting-assistance use; because DNR's UAS-specific application rests on agency interpretation rather than explicit statutory text, a direct inquiry to DNR Wildlife Resources Division is warranted for any use case close to this line.
verification_status: Core statutory text of §§ 27-3-12(a) and 27-3-13 verified directly against Justia's codification; the DNR's UAS-specific interpretation and the feral-hog-only exception characterization are based on secondary industry-compliance and hunting-community sources and were not independently confirmed against a DNR-issued regulation or guidance document in this pass.
notes: Recommend direct verification of DNR's current UAS-specific hunting guidance (regulation or published policy) before citing a specific UAS prohibition to a client, given the gap between the core statutory text and the reported agency interpretation.

geographic_scope: Statewide (all DNR Parks, Recreation, and Historic Sites Division property)
issuing_authority: Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Parks, Recreation and Historic Sites Division
source_title: Drone Prohibition in State Parks and Historic Sites
regulated_activity: Operating a drone within a Georgia state park or historic site
requirement_type: Prohibition, with a Division Director waiver process for commercial/promotional projects
summary: Georgia DNR's published Park Rules & Regulations state that drone operation is prohibited in Georgia's state parks and historic sites. Waivers are occasionally approved for professional commercial projects that may generate revenue or otherwise help promote the sites, but require prior approval from the Division Director. A commercial film/photography request application must detail the project description, specific site location, and exact dates/times of drone use, and must be submitted with FAA drone registration, the pilot's name, and proof of FAA Small UAS Certification or Part 107 certification. Blanket requests are not approved, and drone use is not allowed over populated areas that may put park guests at risk.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Submit a complete commercial film/photography waiver application (project description, site, dates/times, FAA registration, pilot Part 107 certification) to the Division Director well in advance of any AEC UAS work planned within a Georgia state park or historic site, and avoid flight paths over populated guest areas.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Parks, Recreation and Historic Sites Division before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the Division Director's waiver approval in the project file for any state-park or historic-site UAS work; note that blanket or standing approvals are not available, so each project requires its own application.
verification_status: Policy text read directly and in full from Georgia DNR's own published Park Rules & Regulations page.
